newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Prices, new products to decide mobile phone race.
newsitem.headline: Prices, new products to decide mobile phone race.

text.p: Pricing, new products and the ability to tap into emerging markets will determine the winner of the mobile telephone race, which Sweden's Ericsson, America's Motorola Inc. and Finland's Nokia Oy now lead, analysts said Friday.
Just one thing is certain -- competition in this glamorous sector will remain merciless.
The short-term outlook is rosy for the entire mobile telephone industry, with sector leaders set to benefit from rocketing subscriber numbers, which some estimates put at 1 billion by 2001.

"Short term, the market looks great, but we still have worries the environment is going to become more competitive and put pressure on early market entrants like Ericsson, Motorola and Nokia," said Morgan Stanley analyst Angela Dean.

In the meantime, pricing structures, the introduction of more technologically advanced products and a supplier's ability to reach markets with high growth potential can mean a decisive competitive edge, analysts say.

"They are always going to be leapfrogging each other. They all need to have a constant new stream of products coming out on those markets they have decided are important," said Schroeder technology analyst Susan Anthony.
One analyst said Motorola was planning to introduce an agressive pricing structure in the third quarter, stepping up the price war among the three companies and squeezing margins.

Several analysts mentioned the example of the launch of Philips Electronics NV's new lightweight GSM mobile phone, the Genie, planned for later this year. Philips said Thursday the Genie would have a dramatic impact on earnings.
"It's not so easy to break into the market at the current time," said Salomon Brothers analyst Douglas Smith.
"You really have to have economies of scale. Ericsson realised they needed to be a very big player or it wasn't worth being in the business at all," Smith said.

Explosive growth in mobile phone markets drove shares in Sweden's AB LM Ericsson to a record closing high of 353 crowns ($44.61) after it posted stronger-than-expected half-year profits Thursday, and telecommunications industry watchers say they have upgraded expectations for Nokia.

Analysts said Ericsson's 100 percent growth in first-half mobile telephone sales sparked hopes that Nokia would also show handset sales above market estimates when it reports first-half earnings on Aug. 4.
Smith said globalization was a key strategy and noted that one of Ericsson's most valuble markets in the second quarter was Latin America, where it enjoyed growth of 155 percent.
Other players lacked Ericsson's holistic approach, Smith said.

"Lucent has not produced any digital phones yet. The other problem is many companies don't have a global product. Alcatel (of France) and (Germany's) Siemens, who concentrate on the European market, have a much more limited geographical scope."

Analysts have sharpened their focus on the three leading companies' operational mixes. Some believe Ericsson to be better balanced, with traditional fixed telecommunications operations and a leading position in the higher-margin mobile infrastructure business.
But there were gaps in the Swedish giant's armour, Smith said.
"Ericsson does not supply CDMA, which is emerging as a strong standard and that is a hole in their portfolio going forward," said Smith.
CDMA stands for Code Division Multiple Access, a transmission technique that competes with Time Division Multiple Access, or TDMA.
Nokia has greater overall exposure to the fast-growing mobile phone markets, and offers products for a wider range of standards. Motorola's mix includes operations in semiconductors.
Merrill Lynch analyst Neil Barton said that although he expects Nokia, Motorola and Ericsson to remain clear leaders, it was by no means a three-horse race.
"We should not overlook Nortel, Alcatel and Siemens. Philips' objective is to become one of the top three by the year 2000," Barton said.
